lead: An RF passive part stores energy without adding gain: an inductor stores magnetic energy, a capacitor stores electric energy, and a varactor is a capacitor whose value is set by a DC voltage. At radio frequency each part also carries resistance and stray capacitance or inductance, which set its loss, its highest working frequency and its tuning range. Matching networks, filters and voltage-controlled oscillators (VCOs) are built from these parts, so their quality factor Q and self-resonance limit the rest of the unit.
prereq: You need: reactance X<sub>L</sub> = ωL and X<sub>C</sub> = 1/(ωC), series and parallel resonance, and the idea of a matching network from transmission lines and impedance matching.

sections.h3: Quality factor and the on-chip inductor

blocks.text: The quality factor of a reactive part is Q = 2π × (peak energy stored) ÷ (energy lost per cycle). For a part modelled as a reactance X in series with a resistance R, this reduces to Q = |X|/R. High Q means low loss, a sharp resonance and, in an oscillator, low phase noise.

An on-chip inductor is a flat spiral of metal. The spiral gives inductance L in henry. The metal has series resistance R<sub>s</sub> in ohm. The turns couple to each other and to the substrate through a shunt capacitance C<sub>p</sub> in farad. At low frequency the part is simply L in series with R<sub>s</sub>, and its Q rises in proportion to frequency:

blocks.where: ω = 2πf is the angular frequency in rad/s; L is in H; R<sub>s</sub> is in Ω. This is the series-model Q, true only well below self-resonance.

blocks.text: As frequency rises, C<sub>p</sub> carries more current. At the self-resonant frequency f<sub>SR</sub> the inductive and capacitive currents cancel; above it the part behaves as a capacitor.

blocks.where: f<sub>SR</sub> is in Hz. The exact value is a little lower because R<sub>s</sub> damps the resonance.

blocks.text: Including C<sub>p</sub>, the inductor's useful Q is Q<sub>eff</sub> ≈ (ωL/R<sub>s</sub>)[1 − R<sub>s</sub>²C<sub>p</sub>/L − (f/f<sub>SR</sub>)²]. The bracket falls to zero at self-resonance, so Q<sub>eff</sub> rises, peaks and then collapses. Skin effect (R<sub>s</sub> grows roughly as √f) and substrate eddy currents add loss, so real spirals reach Q of only about 5 to 20. Wider metal lowers R<sub>s</sub> but raises C<sub>p</sub>; a rule of thumb is to stay below about half of f<sub>SR</sub>.

A metal-insulator-metal (MIM) capacitor uses two metal layers with a thin insulator between them. It is linear, has a tight tolerance and low series resistance, so it suits filters and matching networks. A MOS capacitor uses a transistor's gate oxide: it is dense and free in a CMOS process, but its value changes with the voltage across it and its channel adds resistance.

blocks.where: C is the capacitance in F; R<sub>s</sub> is the series resistance of the plates, vias and (for a MOS part) the channel, in Ω; ω = 2πf in rad/s.

blocks.text: Capacitor Q falls as frequency rises, the opposite of the inductor. The leads add a series inductance L<sub>s</sub> that resonates with C; above that self-resonance the capacitor looks inductive. Microwave integrated circuits (MMICs) use the same parts.

A varactor is a capacitor whose value is set by a DC control voltage. A diode varactor is a reverse-biased p-n junction: more reverse bias widens the depletion region, so the capacitance falls. (A MOS varactor, used in CMOS VCOs, tunes its gate capacitance between depletion and accumulation.)

blocks.where: C<sub>j0</sub> is the zero-bias capacitance in F; V<sub>R</sub> is the reverse bias in V; φ is the built-in potential, about 0.7 V for silicon; γ is the grading exponent: 1/2 for an abrupt junction, 1/3 for a linearly graded one, and up to about 2 for a hyperabrupt tuning diode.

blocks.text: The capacitance ratio C<sub>max</sub>/C<sub>min</sub> is taken between the two ends of the bias range: C<sub>max</sub> at the smallest reverse bias, C<sub>min</sub> at the largest. In an LC tank f = 1/(2π√(LC)), so the frequency tuning range is only the square root of the capacitance ratio. A small ratio gives a narrow band and a small VCO gain K<sub>VCO</sub> (Hz/V), so control-line noise moves the frequency less.
A varactor's Q = 1/(ωC(V)Rs) is lowest where C is largest. Noise on the control voltage moves C(V) and the frequency, which becomes phase noise; see oscillators and phase noise.

examples.question: A 2 nH on-chip spiral inductor has series resistance R<sub>s</sub> = 4 Ω and shunt capacitance C<sub>p</sub> = 1 pF. At 2 GHz find (a) the series-model Q and the equivalent parallel resistance R<sub>p</sub> ≈ Q²R<sub>s</sub>, (b) the self-resonant frequency, and (c) the effective Q once C<sub>p</sub> is included. Is 2 GHz a sensible operating frequency?
steps: R<sub>p</sub> ≈ Q²R<sub>s</sub> = 6.28² × 4 = 39.48 × 4 = 157.9 Ω. This is the loss resistance the inductor puts across a tank at 2 GHz.

Q<sub>eff</sub> = 6.28 × (1 − 0.008 − 0.316) = 6.28 × 0.676 = 4.25. The impedance of the full model at 2 GHz is 8.50 + j36.1 Ω, and 36.1/8.50 = 4.25 confirms it; the apparent inductance is 36.1/ω = 2.87 nH, not 2 nH.
2 GHz is 0.56 of f<sub>SR</sub>, just above the half-f<sub>SR</sub> rule and near the Q<sub>eff</sub> peak (4.25 at about 2.05 GHz). It works, but the tank must be designed with 2.87 nH and Q = 4.25.
examples.answer: Series-model Q = 6.28 and R<sub>p</sub> ≈ 158 Ω; f<sub>SR</sub> = 3.56 GHz; with C<sub>p</sub> included Q<sub>eff</sub> = 4.25 and the inductance looks like 2.87 nH at 2 GHz.

examples.question: An abrupt-junction varactor (γ = 0.5, φ = 0.7 V) has C<sub>j0</sub> = 2 pF and series resistance 2 Ω. It tunes a tank with L = 5 nH as the reverse bias goes from 1 V to 8 V. Find C<sub>max</sub>, C<sub>min</sub>, the capacitance ratio, the frequency range and the varactor Q at each end.
examples.answer: C runs from 1.283 pF to 0.567 pF (ratio 2.26), the tank tunes from 1.99 GHz to 2.99 GHz (ratio 1.50), and the varactor Q rises from 31.2 at the bottom of the band to 46.9 at the top.

traps: Using Q = ωL/R<sub>s</sub> close to self-resonance. In the worked example it gives 6.28 at 2 GHz while the real value is 4.25; near f<sub>SR</sub> the true Q falls towards zero.
Swapping the formulas: inductor Q = ωL/R<sub>s</sub> rises with frequency; capacitor Q = 1/(ωCR<sub>s</sub>) falls with frequency.
Taking the frequency tuning range equal to the capacitance ratio. A C ratio of 2.26 tunes an LC tank by only √2.26 = 1.50.
Putting C<sub>max</sub> at the largest reverse bias. A reverse-biased junction has its largest capacitance at the smallest bias, because the depletion layer is thinnest.
Calculating a capacitor's reactance as 1/(2πfC) above its series self-resonance, where the part is inductive.

quiz.q: Define the quality factor Q of a reactive part and give the series-model formulas for an inductor and a capacitor.
quiz.a: Q = 2π × peak energy stored ÷ energy lost per cycle. Inductor: Q = ωL/R<sub>s</sub>. Capacitor: Q = 1/(ωCR<sub>s</sub>).

quiz.q: Why does an on-chip spiral stop behaving as an inductor above its self-resonant frequency?
quiz.a: Its shunt capacitance C<sub>p</sub> resonates with L at f<sub>SR</sub>. Above f<sub>SR</sub> the capacitive current is larger than the inductive current, so the impedance is capacitive and Q<sub>eff</sub> is negative.

quiz.q: A MIM capacitor has C = 2 pF and R<sub>s</sub> = 5 Ω. Find its Q at 1 GHz.
An inductor has L = 1 nH and R<sub>s</sub> = 2 Ω. Find its series-model Q at 5 GHz. Does raising L to 2 nH double Q in practice?
quiz.a: Q = 2π × 5 × 10⁹ × 1 × 10⁻⁹/2 = 31.42/2 = 15.7. On paper 2 nH gives 31.4, but a larger spiral has more metal (higher R<sub>s</sub>) and more C<sub>p</sub> (lower f<sub>SR</sub>), so the real Q rises much less than twice.

quiz.q: A VCO's varactor control line picks up noise. Explain how this becomes phase noise and why a smaller capacitance ratio helps.
quiz.a: Noise volts change C(V), which shifts the tank frequency: the carrier is frequency-modulated by the noise, which shows up as phase-noise sidebands. A smaller C ratio gives a smaller K<sub>VCO</sub>, so the same noise voltage moves the frequency less, at the cost of a narrower tuning band.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern VCOs pair a bank of switched MIM capacitors for coarse tuning with a small varactor for fine tuning, keeping K<sub>VCO</sub> low and Q high. Spirals are designed with electromagnetic field solvers and patterned ground shields. Search for 'patterned ground shield inductor' and 'switched capacitor bank VCO'.

figure.caption: The worked example's 2 nH spiral: its 1 pF shunt capacitance resonates at 3.56 GHz, so the real Q (solid) peaks near 2 GHz at 4.25 and falls to zero at self-resonance, while the simple ωL/R<sub>s</sub> (dashed) keeps rising to 6.28 and beyond.

spec.aria: Left, the inductor model: a 4 ohm resistor in series with 2 nanohenries, with 1 picofarad across both. Right, Q against frequency from 0 to 4 gigahertz. The dashed straight line omega L over Rs reaches 6.28 at 2 gigahertz. The solid curve including Cp peaks at 4.25 near 2 gigahertz and falls to zero at the self-resonant frequency of 3.56 gigahertz.
